executive_summary: The defining thread across today's content is the question of how established institutions — religious, political, and international — are responding to forces that threaten to outpace their authority and coherence. Pope Leo's Sunday warning on artificial intelligence marks a significant moment of institutional intervention, as the Catholic Church positions itself as a moral arbiter in a technological debate that secular governance has struggled to regulate. This mirrors the anxieties running through the Foreign Affairs newsletters, where the concept of 'middle power delusion' and Saudi Arabia's hedging strategy both reflect nations grappling with a world order in which traditional levers of institutional power — alliances, sovereignty, ideological alignment — are losing their reliability. The Economist's 'Don't panic, but be prepared' framing reinforces the same undercurrent: that the institutions and frameworks societies have historically relied upon for stability are under stress, and the question is not whether disruption is coming but whether leadership can respond with enough clarity and speed to matter. Taken together, today's content delivers a consistent warning that the gap between the pace of change and the capacity of institutions to manage it is widening, and that gap itself is the central risk of the moment.

items.headline: Don't panic! (But be prepared)
items.blurb: Ramping up defence capacity—and how to pay for it—has been a major headache for NATO's European members for years now. Recently Tim Judah has been working on the issue of British civil defence. That includes things like air-raid shelters, which we don't have, and advising the public on what they should do if war comes, which we don't do. The Nordics, the Baltics and Poland have all been stepping up civil-defence planning since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Defence experts say that the real problem is that, unlike Sweden, Britain hasn't put a dedicated minister in charge, and so preparations remain dispersed and unco-ordinated. Food is a major vulnerability. Britain imports 40-50% of what it needs, but that is channelled through a very few ports. We have no government food stocks.

items.blurb: Shashank has been in Washington, DC, interviewing Bill Burns, the former CIA director, for the next episode of Inside Defence. You can watch that at 6pm London time tomorrow.

items.headline: Roasted Rhubarb
items.blurb: Cooked slowly in the oven, the stalks turn tender and compote-like, but the steady heat helps the pieces keep their shape. Add vanilla, spices or citrus zest if you'd like, or leave it plain, letting the bracing flavor of rhubarb shine.

items.headline: Grilled Honey-Mustard Chicken Thighs
items.blurb: Is your grill still set up from the weekend? Put it to good use with Lidey Heuck's boneless chicken thighs glazed with Dijon for sharpness, honey for sweetness and Worcestershire for a salty tang. Or cook the chicken under the broiler to achieve a similar char.

items.headline: Cumin Tofu Stir-Fry
items.blurb: Spicy and speedy, you can make Hetty McKinnon's gutsy stir-fry with whatever chile flakes you have on hand — gochugaru (Korean red chile flakes), crushed red pepper or Sichuan pepper flakes each add their own particular zip to the dish. I'm a fan of Sichuan pepper, both numbing and fiery. Serve this over rice to balance the heat.

items.headline: Toasted Coconut Rice Salad
items.blurb: The depth of flavor in Kayla Hoang's crunchy salad comes from toasting jasmine rice before cooking it in coconut milk. Then the fragrant, lightly sweet rice gets tossed with shredded purple cabbage, cashews and a sprightly ginger dressing for a contrasting bite.

items.headline: Harissa Shrimp with Greens and Feta
items.blurb: Broiling shrimp is a terrific way to sear them quickly and deeply, so their insides stay juicy and the edges get a little singed. In this sheet-pan recipe, Yewande Komolafe broils shrimp coated in a zesty, garlicky harissa marinade. Then she serves them over greens along with avocado, red onions and feta for a colorful meal to brighten any weeknight.

items.headline: The Only Ice Cream Recipe You'll Ever Need
items.blurb: This flexible ice cream can be as rich or as light as you'd like depending on the ratio of heavy cream to whole milk you use to make the custard. Then flavor it with whatever you fancy — anything from vanilla beans to fruit, caramel, chocolate or pistachios. Homemade ice cream is always better than what you can buy, and the vanilla version tastes especially great with that roasted rhubarb.

items.headline: Wait, those teams are leading MLB?
items.blurb: The season is upending conventional wisdom, which is always pretty fun. Several underdog rosters are thriving in the final year of the collective bargaining agreement between the owners and players. The Brewers lead the National League Central. The Rays lead the American League East. The Guardians lead the AL Central. The Athletics, who play in West Sacramento, lead the AL West. Their payroll rankings, according to Spotrac: 20th (Brewers), 21st (Athletics), 28th (Guardians), 29th (Rays).

items.headline: Fritz's awkward French Open result
items.blurb: U.S. men logged a milestone in Paris yesterday: Wild card Nishesh Basavareddy won his first-round match 7-6(5), 7-6(5), 6-7(9), 6-1 for the first victory for an American man over a top-10 opponent at the French Open since 2000. The problem? Basavareddy's opponent was a compatriot: No. 7 seed Taylor Fritz.
